title: Can deterministic LOCAL coloring use a near-linear palette in log-star n rounds?
formal: Do there exist absolute constants K,C and one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that, for every simple n-vertex graph and supplied maximum-degree bound $\Delta\ge2$, outputs a proper coloring with at most $\lceil K\Delta^{1.001}\rceil$ colors in at most $C(1+\log^*n)$ rounds? Vertices know n and Delta and have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. Neither K nor C may depend on Delta or n.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform algorithm and constants, or prove that no such constants and algorithm exist. A log-star n bound with a degree-dependent hidden constant does not settle this proposition.
context:
A fast coloring algorithm can allow itself more colors than a sequential greedy algorithm. The extra palette gives neighboring vertices more room to make independent choices. This question fixes an extremely short round budget and asks how much extra palette is actually necessary.

The exponent 1.001 makes the requested palette slightly superlinear in maximum degree. It is still much smaller than a quadratic palette for sufficiently large degree. Because the graph family ranges over every degree, hiding a large degree-dependent factor in the running time would erase the intended tradeoff.

For example, fixing degree first and then saying that an algorithm takes a constant number of rounds is insufficient: that constant might grow as the degree squared. The question instead requires one numerical multiplier on log-star n that works as both graph size and degree grow. This is why all the constants are quantified explicitly.

Classical color reduction reaches a quadratic-degree palette in iterated-logarithmic time. The source lists reducing the palette below that quadratic scale, and in particular to degree raised to 1.001, as unresolved. The card focuses on that one concrete target; optimal Delta+1 coloring with a larger degree-dependent round budget is a separate question.
why: I include this because it separates the cost of symmetry breaking from the number of colors used to absorb local conflicts. A solution would clarify whether the quadratic palette in a foundational distributed primitive reflects an intrinsic limitation or merely the current method of reducing identifiers to colors.
definitions: Proper means that every input edge has differently colored endpoints. Colors are integers from one shared palette. The identifier bound has a fixed polynomial range in n. Log-star uses base two. The target is deterministic worst-case elapsed rounds over graphs and valid identifier assignments. Delta is not treated as a fixed constant outside the asymptotic bound.

progress.text: Linial’s color reduction gives an $O(\Delta^2)$-coloring in $O(\log^*n)$ rounds. Symmetry-breaking lower bounds also show that the graph-size dependence cannot in general become o(log-star n) when degree is fixed.
Maus and Tonoyan revisit the local color-reduction method and extend it to list and conflict constraints. Their result does not establish the near-linear palette at the requested uniform round bound.
Suomela explicitly lists the Delta-to-the-1.001 palette target within O(log-star n) deterministic rounds.
